sources.entry: Traffic Management: A Holistic Approach to Memory Placement on NUMA Systems - Proves against the kernel balancer that controller and link congestion, not remote latency, is what placement manages.

summary.title: Traffic Management: A Holistic Approach to Memory Placement on NUMA Systems
summary.one_liner: Modern NUMA performance is limited by memory controller and interconnect congestion rather than remote access latency, so placement must manage traffic using a mix of interleaving, replication, and co-location (the Carrefour algorithm).
takeaways: On modern NUMA hardware, remote wire delay adds at most about 30% to memory access cost, so congestion on memory controllers and interconnects matters more for performance.
Better locality does not always improve performance: interleaving reduced local access ratio for PCA yet improved its performance, because it cut memory latency via lower congestion.
Carrefour combines page co-location, interleaving, replication and thread clustering, chosen per application from global traffic statistics and per-page sampled access patterns.

Carrefour's decision thresholds in the paper include MAPTU above 50, replication only with a 95% memory read ratio and enough free RAM, interleaving when controller imbalance exceeds 35%, and co-location when local access ratio is below 80%.
Reported results: up to 3.6x speedup over the default Linux kernel, and no more than 4% slowdown when placement cannot be improved.
summary.summary: The paper argues that on modern NUMA systems, congestion in memory controllers and interconnect links, driven by data-intensive applications, hurts performance far more than remote access latency. The authors measure this with local versus remote single-thread runs and with first-touch versus interleaving policies on multi-threaded benchmarks from NAS, PARSEC and Metis, backed by hardware counter data on latency, imbalance and IPC. They then present Carrefour, a Linux algorithm with measurement, global decision and page-local decision components that enables interleaving, replication and co-location based on defined thresholds. The paper reports up to 3.6x speedup over the default kernel and a worst-case slowdown of about 4%, and it is written for an academic systems audience.
